Ghosting as Control.short_definition: Going completely silent without explanation, then reappearing later, which leaves the other person with open questions and nothing to close them.
Ghosting as Control.core_meaning: Going completely silent without explanation, then reappearing later, which leaves the other person with open questions and nothing to close them.
Ghosting as Control.expanded_definition: Ghosting is when contact stops all at once, with no reason given and no reply to direct questions. Ghosting as control describes the version where the silence does a job: it keeps attention fixed on the person who went quiet, and it tends to end when the other person starts to move on, with a message that acts as if nothing happened. Many people ghost out of discomfort, so a single disappearance says very little. What turns it into a pattern is the timing and the repeat.
Ghosting as Control.plain_language_summary: Someone vanishes without a word, leaves you guessing, and then turns up again just when you have started to put it behind you.
Ghosting as Control.why_this_matters: With no account of what happened, there is nothing to work through. The questions stay open, and your attention stays tied to someone who is no longer answering. Closure usually takes two people's words, and here you are left to write both sides yourself.
what_it_is: A complete stop to texts, calls and replies after a stretch of regular contact, with no goodbye and no reason.
Silence that carries on even when you ask directly, once or several times, whether something is wrong.
Often followed by a return, such as a casual 'hey stranger' message, that skips over the gap as if it were nothing.
Seen in dating and friendships, and also with family members, former partners and co-parents who stop answering for stretches.
Different from a plain ending, even a painful one: here the missing explanation is what keeps the person waiting.
what_it_sounds_like: Three weeks of no replies, then: Hey you! Sorry, life got crazy.
A read receipt and nothing else for days, after you asked whether you had done something.
Saw you got a new job, congrats! Want to catch up?, arriving right after you mentioned moving on.
Your calls go to voicemail, but a mutual friend says they were at a party that weekend.
I just needed space. Why are you making it a big deal?
A like on an old photo months later, with no message attached.
Oh, you're still upset about that? It was ages ago.
what_it_is_not: Someone who says 'I need distance right now' and then stays distant. Even a short line like that is an explanation, and it ends the guessing.
A person who finds every hard conversation so uncomfortable that they avoid all of them, with everyone, not only you.
A friendship or romance that faded by mutual drift, where neither side chased and neither felt dropped.
A pause forced by circumstances such as a hospital stay, a lost phone, a bereavement or a posting with no signal.
Going quiet yourself to stay away from someone who is unsafe. That is a sound choice and not this pattern.
this_may_be_it_when: The silence began suddenly after a long run of steady, warm contact.
Direct questions about what happened go unanswered, though the person is plainly active elsewhere.
Messages come back soon after you mention a new job, a new relationship or a decision to move on.
When they return, the gap is never acknowledged, and your questions about it are brushed aside.
The cycle of vanishing and returning has happened more than once, with similar timing.
this_may_not_be_it_when: They gave a reason, even a brief or clumsy one, such as needing space or being overwhelmed.
They are quiet with everyone in their life, and friends report the same.
They come back and say what happened and own the gap without being asked.
A clear event, like illness, travel or a lost phone, accounts for the quiet.
The contact was only ever occasional, so this silence is closer to its usual rhythm than a break.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Some people shut down when they feel guilty or overwhelmed and cannot find the words, so they say nothing.
A burst of work, family trouble or a low stretch can cut off replies to everyone.
Online friendships and dating-app matches often end without a goodbye because neither side felt it owed one.
Phones break, accounts lock and messages get lost.
common_false_positives: A date who never texted back after one meeting, where nothing was promised.
A friend who has always been slow to reply in every season of life.
An ex who stopped all contact after you asked them to, and whose silence has simply stayed stopped.
discernment_questions: Did they offer any reason, even a short one, or was it silence from start to finish?
Do they go quiet with other people too, or only with me?
When contact returns, does it line up with moments when I seemed to be moving on?
If I ask what happened, do I get an answer, or does the question get waved off?
Is my life on hold while I wait, or have I been able to carry on?
less_concerning_if: The silence lasted days rather than months, and an explanation came when it ended.
It was a one-off, and the friendship or relationship carried on at its usual pace afterward.
Their habit of avoiding conflict is open and familiar, and you have seen it with other people too.
more_concerning_if: Silence and return repeat in a cycle, and each return comes with warmth that expects a quick welcome back.
Practical matters such as shared bills or a child's pickup are left hanging while the silence runs.
Contact resumes only when you start to build something new, and stops again if you do not answer at once.
pattern_over_time_signs: You check your phone more than you want to, and open the thread to see whether it has been read.
You have drafted messages you never send, explaining yourself to someone who never asked.
Friends notice you putting plans on hold in case the person reappears.
Their return has started to feel like weather: you cannot predict it, but you organize your days around it.
Ghosting as Control.repair_check: Repair here starts with an account of the gap: what happened, why no word came, and what they will do differently, such as sending one line next time they need distance. A warm 'miss you!' that skips over the silence only restarts the wait.
Ghosting as Control.boundary_respect_check: Compare two outcomes after you tell them the silence hurt. A heads-up such as 'I need a few days' before the next quiet spell means your point landed. Another unannounced silence, or being called too needy for asking, means it did not.
Ghosting as Control.psychological_mechanism: Not knowing tends to keep the mind working on a problem that never closes. People often replay the last conversation looking for a cause, and that rumination can become a kind of tie to the other person. Returns that arrive at unpredictable times can also strengthen the pull, because rewards that come unpredictably tend to hold attention more than steady ones.
Ghosting as Control.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe checking their phone through the night, rewriting what they said, wondering what they did, and feeling embarrassed at still caring. Some put plans on hold in case the person comes back. Others describe anger that arrives later, once they see that the silence said nothing true about their worth.

response_options.soft_clarification: Send one short, open message you can stand behind: 'I noticed we stopped talking. I'd like to understand, but I can accept not getting an answer.' Then let it rest.
response_options.firm_boundary: Tell them what you need: 'If you step away again, I'd like a line saying so. If that is not possible, I will treat the silence as an ending.'
response_options.disengagement: Treat the silence as the answer you have, even though it is an incomplete one. Mute the thread, archive it, and write the closing note to yourself rather than to them.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell a friend exactly what you keep replaying and ask what they see from outside. Saying the loop out loud often shrinks it.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If a colleague, client or co-parent goes silent on matters you share, move that part to a written channel with dates, such as email or a shared task list, so the work does not depend on their replies.

Ghosting as Control.boundary_script: "When you stopped replying, I was left guessing. I'm not asking you to explain everything. I'm asking that next time you need distance, you tell me in one line, so I'm not left waiting."
Ghosting as Control.safety_note: Silence alone is not a safety signal. What would change that is attention that turns to watching. That is a person who ignores your messages but appears at your workplace, follows your accounts closely, or sends word through other people. If that begins, keep a dated log of each instance and talk to an advocate before you reply to anything.
misuse_warning: Calling every unreturned message ghosting turns busy people and mismatched interest into accused offenders. The label needs a pattern of vanishing and returning, not one quiet week.
The word 'control' says something about the other person's goal that you cannot see from here. What you can observe is the timing and the unanswered questions.
Ghosting as Control.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Ghosting as Control is absence, while Stalking & Surveillance (Post-Separation) is constant presence or awareness, even when no word is said. Forced Submission pushes hard for an apology or confession, where ghosting gives you nothing to answer at all. A Smear Campaign talks about you to other people; ghosting leaves the reason unspoken to everyone. What sets this one apart is silence that lifts when you begin to move on.

Humiliation Rituals.short_definition: A repeated, formal practice of diminishing people in front of others, presented as initiation, correction or growth, where the pain is treated as proof it works.
Humiliation Rituals.core_meaning: A repeated, formal practice of diminishing people in front of others, presented as initiation, correction or growth, where the pain is treated as proof it works.
Humiliation Rituals.expanded_definition: Humiliation rituals are routines inside a team, school, program or group in which people are made to look small before an audience, through costumes, forced confessions, public rankings or mock trials, and are told it builds character or trust. The ritual has a script, a place and often a calendar, which gives it the look of tradition. A tough exercise or one bad day proves little. It becomes a ritual when the diminishing is regular, everyone is expected to take part, and objecting counts as failing.
Humiliation Rituals.plain_language_summary: A group makes members or newcomers look foolish in front of others, again and again, and says it is how they grow. Saying it hurts is treated as proof you are not up to it.
Humiliation Rituals.why_this_matters: Being told the humiliation is the point makes objecting look like failing the test. The cost gets paid twice: once in front of the group, and again in staying silent about it afterward.
what_it_is: A routine with a fixed form, such as a nickname round, a costume day, a public confession or a ranking read aloud, repeated for each new person or each cycle.
An audience built into the design: the diminishing happens before peers, a class, a team or a congregation.
A stated purpose, such as toughening up, bonding, accountability or personal growth, offered whenever someone questions it.
Found in sports teams, clubs, military-style programs, workplaces, schools, coaching groups and some self-improvement or faith settings.
Pain or shame treated as evidence the process is working, so discomfort can never count as a reason to stop.
what_it_sounds_like: Everyone goes through this. It's how we build character.
If you can't take this, you won't make it here.
Stand up and tell the room what you did wrong this week.
A new hire made to wear a ridiculous outfit for the first month while everyone watches.
The people who complained are the ones who needed it most.
Thank them. They're helping you get better.
A weekly meeting where each member's mistakes are read out and the group votes on a penalty.
what_it_is_not: Hard training and demanding standards that push people without diminishing them. Sore legs and long hours are not shame.
One harsh moment inside an otherwise respectful process, which is friction and not a rite.
Frank critique given privately, or in a group where everyone agreed to the format and can pass.
A playful tradition that people can decline at no cost, such as a silly-hat day nobody is made to join.
A vulnerability exercise where the leader goes first, everyone shares failures, and anyone may skip a turn.
this_may_be_it_when: The same ritual is run for every newcomer or every cycle, regardless of what any one person did.
Embarrassment before others is the core of the activity and not a side effect.
People who say it is too much are told they are weak, ungrateful or not committed.
Veterans describe it fondly as something they endured, and expect the next group to endure it.
Nobody can say what skill or bond it builds, other than that you will understand later.
this_may_not_be_it_when: People can opt out or ask to change the activity without losing standing.
The leaders take part in the same exercises on the same terms.
The feedback is about the work and names a specific thing to fix.
No audience is needed; the exercise would work the same way one-to-one.
Objections lead to adjustments, and the group changes the practice when it hurts people.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Groups pass on traditions they inherited without thinking about how they land, and the people running them may remember their own time as fun.
Teasing that close teammates have accepted can look cruel to outsiders and still be mutual.
Some intense programs are built around stamina, and the discomfort comes from the task and not from being watched.
A light ceremony, such as a roast the guest of honor agreed to, can sting a little and still be welcome.
common_false_positives: A comedy-style roast where the guest of honor volunteered and everyone else gets roasted too.
A boot camp or preseason where everyone suffers equally and nobody is held up for ridicule.
A manager's blunt feedback in a one-to-one meeting, which stings but is not staged for anyone else.
discernment_questions: Would the stated lesson still land if the audience were taken away?
Who decided this was part of the program, and can anyone say no to it?
Do the people running it go through it too?
When someone objects, does anything change, or is the objection read as weakness?
Do I feel closer to the group afterward, or smaller and quieter?
Is it applied the same way to everyone, or do some people get more of it?
less_concerning_if: People can decline an activity and keep their place in the group.
The practice has been changed or dropped after members said it was too much.
The activity has a stated skill goal, and members can say what they learned from it.
more_concerning_if: Declining costs a place on the team, a grade, a reference or a job.
Photos, video or posts of the ritual circulate beyond the group.
Physical discomfort, forced consumption, sleeplessness or exposure to the elements is part of the ritual.
pattern_over_time_signs: Each new cohort is handed the same routine, and last year's recipients help run it.
You start to dread a particular day of the week or a particular meeting.
Members stop speaking up about anything, because the last person who did became the next example.
Stories about the ritual are told as jokes, while privately people admit it still stings.
Humiliation Rituals.repair_check: Fixing this means the practice itself changes: the activity is altered or dropped, the people it hit are asked what it was like, and nobody is told they took it the wrong way. A heartfelt speech followed by the same ritual next term is only a speech.
Humiliation Rituals.boundary_respect_check: Your standing is the gauge once you say a part was too much. An adjusted activity and unchanged treatment of you suggest the concern registered. A new nickname, lost assignments, or a turn as the next example suggest the objection was folded into the test.
Humiliation Rituals.psychological_mechanism: Public shame can make a person want to belong more, not less, because the group is both the source of the pain and the place to be accepted. When pain is framed as the price of membership, people often defend it afterward, partly to avoid concluding they suffered for nothing. Each cohort that completes it can then pass it on.
Humiliation Rituals.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe dread before the scheduled day, replaying the moment in their heads, and shame that lingers after the group has moved on. Some describe fierce loyalty alongside a private sense of being smaller. Others go quiet in meetings, and some feel real anger years later when they see what was done.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask about purpose in an even tone: 'What is this exercise meant to teach, and could we do it without everyone watching?' The answer shows whether the lesson needs the audience.
response_options.firm_boundary: Ask for a neutral person, such as a program coordinator, faculty advisor or HR contact, to sit in on the next session and hear how it is run.
response_options.disengagement: Without announcing anything, keep a private record of dates, what was asked and who was present, and avoid sharing or forwarding images of the ritual.
response_options.support_seeking: Talk with someone who went through the same program but is no longer inside it, and compare what each of you remembers. Shared recall makes it harder to dismiss your own.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Check the written code of conduct or the hazing and harassment policy, then take a dated written account to HR, an ombudsperson (an independent complaints officer), a student affairs office or an advisor.

Humiliation Rituals.boundary_script: "I'm trying to understand what this part is meant to build. Could someone from outside the group, like the program coordinator, come along next time, so we can all talk about how it's run?"
Humiliation Rituals.safety_note: Watch for physical risk inside the ritual: forced drinking or eating, sleep deprivation, exposure to cold or heat, restraint, or dares with a chance of injury. Photos used as leverage matter too. If anyone is hurt or in danger of being hurt, call local emergency services. Otherwise, bring a written account to a coordinator, ombudsperson or student-conduct office.
misuse_warning: Calling a tough team culture a humiliation ritual erases the line between hard and degrading. Ask whether people are being made smaller before an audience, not whether the standards are high.
Applying the term to one tasteless joke or one harsh review makes the word loud and the pattern invisible.
Humiliation Rituals.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Public Humiliation can be a single episode of embarrassing someone in front of others, while Humiliation Rituals recur on a schedule, cover a whole cohort and arrive with a stated purpose. Forced Submission centers on getting an apology or confession from one person, but a ritual may ask for no words at all, only that you endure it. A Smear Campaign spreads claims about a person to others, whereas here the audience watches the act itself.

Forced Submission.short_definition: Pressing someone to apologize, confess or comply until they give in, whether or not the facts support it.
Forced Submission.core_meaning: Pressing someone to apologize, confess or comply until they give in, whether or not the facts support it.
Forced Submission.expanded_definition: Forced submission is pressure that keeps going until a person says the required words or does the required thing, whether or not they believe it. The apology, confession or signature becomes the goal, and the question of what happened drops away. It can arise in a family, a workplace, a school or a hearing. One heated demand for an apology is common after a hurt. It turns into this when the pressure outlasts every explanation and the person finally complies to make it stop.
Forced Submission.plain_language_summary: You are pushed again and again to say sorry or admit to something until you give in, even when nobody has checked whether you did it.
Forced Submission.why_this_matters: An apology given to end pressure still enters the record as an admission, and the person then has to live alongside having confessed to something they do not believe they did. Coerced words can also be quoted back at them later.
what_it_is: A demand for an apology, confession or signed statement that continues after the person has explained their account.
An end to the pressure that is on offer only in exchange for the words: 'say it and we can move on'.
Refusal read as further proof of guilt, so denial makes things worse.
Seen at kitchen tables, in staff meetings, in schools, at disciplinary hearings and in groups with a clear hierarchy.
Different from asking for accountability: here the facts are not tested before the words are required.
what_it_sounds_like: Just say you're sorry and this can be over.
I'm not leaving this room until you admit it.
Sign this statement and we'll drop it.
Every time you deny it, it gets worse for you.
If you really cared, you'd apologize. Apologize.
Say it like you mean it. Again.
Nobody is asking whether you did it. We're asking you to own it.
what_it_is_not: Asking for accountability where something did happen. Saying you were hurt and want it acknowledged is not forcing anything.
A manager or teacher requiring a written account of an incident, with a chance to give your side.
A parent asking a young child to say sorry to a sibling, as a lesson in manners and not as an admission of a disputed fact.
A heartfelt apology you choose to give after thinking it over, even if a friend gently prompted it.
A settlement or mediation outcome that both sides sign after each has had their say.
this_may_be_it_when: The pressure continues after you have given a clear, consistent account.
The demand is for words and not for a fix: no one asks what would repair the damage.
Your denial is treated as an added offense.
You give in at the end and later think, I don't actually believe that.
The same method is used on other people in that setting, and those who gave in are held up as models.
this_may_not_be_it_when: Your side was asked for and listened to before anything was requested of you.
You can say 'I disagree' and the matter is allowed to rest.
What is being asked for matches something you agree did happen.
The request has a clear end: once an apology is given, the conversation does close.
Someone outside the exchange reviewed the facts and reached the same finding.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Someone who is hurt may press hard for acknowledgment because being heard matters to them, without doubting anything you say.
In a stressful moment people repeat a demand because they are upset, and ease off after a break.
Workplaces and schools have standard forms and statements that feel coercive but are routine.
Apologizing for how something landed, when you never meant harm, is a normal part of repair and is not a confession of wrongdoing.
common_false_positives: A friend who says 'I need you to acknowledge this hurt me' once, and accepts your answer.
A court or HR process that asks everyone involved for a written statement.
Siblings pushed to shake hands after a fight.
discernment_questions: Has anyone asked what happened before asking what I will say?
Does the pressure stop when I give an account, or only when I give the words?
Would I say this if no one were pressing me?
If I refuse, is that treated as a fresh offense?
Is a record being kept of what I say, and who can see it?
Can I take time to think, or must it be now?
less_concerning_if: You were allowed to give your side and a pause was accepted.
The wording of any apology was left to you.
The matter closed once you said it and was not brought up again.
more_concerning_if: A signature, recorded statement or written admission is what is required, and it may be kept on file.
The person pressing also controls something you rely on, such as your job, your housing or your time with your child.
You feel afraid of what happens if you keep saying no.
pattern_over_time_signs: You apologize quickly now, to avoid the pressure, even for things you do not think you did.
Past apologies are quoted back to you as proof of what you did.
You have learned which words end the conversation, and you say them without meaning them.
You find it hard to tell, even privately, what you actually believe about the original event.
Forced Submission.repair_check: Someone asking, after the fact, what really happened, and accepting your account where it checks out, is what mending looks like here. Withdrawing a coerced admission from any record is the strongest sign. Being thanked for finally 'coming around' is not repair.
Forced Submission.boundary_respect_check: Try giving your account once, calmly, and then stop. Notice whether the talk turns to what could be done about it, or whether the demand for the words simply gets louder. How the pressure responds to a finished answer is the information.
Forced Submission.psychological_mechanism: Sustained pressure can make the end of discomfort more attractive than being right. Words said to stop it can then start to feel chosen, which can blur what the person actually believes. Exhaustion, an audience, or having no way out of the room tends to speed this along. A written or spoken confession can also pull later memory toward the confessed version.
Forced Submission.possible_impact_on_receiver: Giving in is often followed by a sick feeling, anger at oneself, and doubt about what one truly thinks of the original event. Some find they apologize automatically afterward. Others dread any conflict, because they expect it to end the same way, with their own words used against them.

response_options.soft_clarification: Offer your account once and ask for a way forward: 'Here is what I remember. What would help put it right?' Moving to repair can shift the talk from words to actions.
response_options.firm_boundary: If it feels safe, decline to say words you do not believe: 'I can apologize for how it landed. I can't say I did something I don't think I did.'
response_options.disengagement: Take a break from a conversation that has become a loop, and come back to it in writing, where nothing has to be answered on the spot.
response_options.support_seeking: Before signing or saying anything formal, tell someone outside the situation what is being asked and read it aloud to them. A second pair of ears can hear coercion that you can no longer hear.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: At work or school, ask what the process is, who will read the statement and what happens afterward. Ask to give your account in your own words, in writing, and keep a copy.

Forced Submission.boundary_script: "I've told you what I remember. I can say I'm sorry it hurt you, because I am. I can't say I did something I don't believe I did, and I'd rather work out together what would help."
Forced Submission.safety_note: Pressure to apologize is not a danger signal on its own. It changes when fear is part of the picture: shouting that blocks a doorway, threats toward your job, housing or children, or a written confession demanded on the spot. If so, avoid signing anything in the moment and ask a legal aid service or an advocate to read it first.
misuse_warning: Calling any request for an apology forced submission can let real accountability slide. When something did happen, asking for acknowledgment is fair.
Using the label for being asked to follow an agreed rule treats ordinary limits as coercion.
Forced Submission.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Humiliation Rituals diminish people before an audience whether or not words are demanded, while forced submission can happen in a private room with one person and ends with a statement. Public Humiliation is about exposure to others, but here the exchange runs until the person speaks. Ghosting as Control withholds speech altogether; this one demands it.

Stalking & Surveillance (Post-Separation.short_definition: Repeated watching, tracking or following of a former partner after a breakup, in person or through phones and accounts, leaving them unable to live unobserved.
Stalking & Surveillance (Post-Separation.core_meaning: Repeated watching, tracking or following of a former partner after a breakup, in person or through phones and accounts, leaving them unable to live unobserved.
Stalking & Surveillance (Post-Separation.expanded_definition: Stalking and surveillance overlap, but they are not the same. Stalking is repeated unwanted following, contact or appearing where you are. Surveillance is the monitoring: location tracking, access to accounts, questions put to friends or relatives. Either can appear without the other. Because shared custody and mutual friends make some contact normal, a single run-in or piece of news says almost nothing. What stands out is knowledge or presence that fits no channel you chose to open.
Stalking & Surveillance (Post-Separation.plain_language_summary: After a relationship ends, the other person keeps showing up, tracking you, or knowing things about your life that you never told them.
Stalking & Surveillance (Post-Separation.why_this_matters: Separation is supposed to end the other person's access. When it does not, ordinary life, including where you live, who you see and what you do next, goes on under observation, and nowhere feels fully private.
what_it_is: Following or turning up: waiting outside a home or workplace, appearing at places you go regularly, driving past.
Digital watching: location sharing left on, an unfamiliar app or tracker on a device, shared cloud or family-plan logins that were never switched off.
Indirect watching: questions to friends, coworkers, children or relatives about where you are and who you are with.
Contact that goes on after it has been declined, including messages from new numbers or accounts.
Knowledge of your plans or whereabouts that cannot be traced to anything you shared.
Two behaviors that often travel together after a breakup, watching and approaching, though either can happen alone.
what_it_sounds_like: I saw you at the grocery store on Saturday. Nice jacket. (You told them nothing about your weekend.)
How was dinner with your sister? (You never mentioned it.)
The same car parked across from your building more than once.
Messages arriving from a new number minutes after you blocked the old one.
A friend says: they keep asking me where you are and who you're seeing.
A device you never set up shows in your list of signed-in devices.
I just happened to be in the area.
what_it_is_not: Shared custody and shared property need real, continuing contact: handoffs, schedules, a lease, a car loan.
News traveling through mutual friends, with nobody asking or monitoring anyone.
A former partner who sees you at the same gym or town event, says hello and moves on, in a small community.
Public posts that anyone could read. Seeing what you chose to post openly is not tracking.
A co-parenting arrangement in which both parents agreed to share a child's location.
Lingering fear of being watched after real contact has ended. It is common and deserves support, and it is not always evidence of present monitoring.
this_may_be_it_when: They know details you never told them, and your mutual friends deny passing them on.
They appear at your home, work, gym or a child's school with no logistical reason.
Contact continues after you asked for it to stop, shifting to new numbers, accounts or messengers.
A device, account or location setting turns out to be shared or accessed without your say.
The attention rises when something in your life changes, such as a move, a new job or a new relationship.
this_may_not_be_it_when: Their contact stays inside shared logistics, such as exchange times and bills, and ends once those are settled.
What they know came from something you posted openly or from a friend who passed it on openly.
Run-ins happen in a place you both have an ordinary reason to be.
They have respected the end of contact, and any request to stop, for months.
A neutral technician checked your devices and accounts and found nothing unfamiliar.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: In a small town or shared social circle, former partners meet often by chance.
Mutual friends talk, and news about your life can reach your ex without anyone being asked.
Shared accounts, family phone plans or old logins can leave access open simply because nobody closed them.
Co-parents may need to know pickup times and school events.
common_false_positives: A former partner who messages about the children's schedule and nothing else.
A shared streaming or cloud account that shows old photos or viewing history because nobody closed it.
A mutual friend who repeats what they saw on your public page without being asked to.
discernment_questions: Does this person know things I never told them, and can I trace how?
Does contact about shared children or property stay on those subjects?
Has the attention grown since we separated, instead of fading?
Do I know which devices and accounts are signed in to my life, and who shares them?
Do I change where I go, or when, because I expect to be seen?
Has anyone else noticed the car, the messages or the questions?
less_concerning_if: Contact is limited to scheduled exchanges and stops when each exchange is over.
Whatever they know can be traced to something public or something a friend said openly.
Time has reduced the contact rather than raised it.
more_concerning_if: They appear at places you did not announce, or know your plans in advance.
Contact has increased since you ended things, or since a new relationship, move or job.
There have been threats, damage to property, or messages that hint at what they know about your movements.
pattern_over_time_signs: You change your route, your hours or your gym without a practical reason.
You check mirrors, windows and parking lots more than you used to, and dread opening a new message.
Friends and relatives report being questioned about you, in small amounts, over many months.
Moments when your life changes, such as a new apartment or partner, are followed by a rise in the signs.
Stalking & Surveillance (Post-Separation.repair_check: Distance that holds over months is the sign to look for: contact narrows to logistics, the questions to friends stop, and nothing surfaces that they should not know. A promise to stop followed by a message from a new number is not it.
Stalking & Surveillance (Post-Separation.boundary_respect_check: Treat the hours and days after any limit you set as the data. A gradual silence that holds is one kind of answer. New numbers, messages through friends, anger, or more precise knowledge of your movements is another, and a reason to involve an advocate before anything else.
Stalking & Surveillance (Post-Separation.psychological_mechanism: Knowing you may be watched can change behavior even when nothing visible happens, because a person begins to plan around where the other might be. Uncertainty about what is known, and how, tends to wear down the sense of private space. Surprises, such as being quoted something you never shared, can make the watching feel larger than any single incident.
Stalking & Surveillance (Post-Separation.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe checking locks and parking lots, changing routes or phones, sleeping badly and flinching at new notifications. Some stop going to places they love. Others describe being told they are imagining it, and feeling more alone for it. Many describe relief when someone helps them document what is happening.

response_options.soft_clarification: Notice and note first. Write down what they knew, when, and how it could have reached them. Hold off on asking them how they know; an advocate can help you decide whether asking is safe.
response_options.firm_boundary: Keep necessary contact to one written channel and to the shared subject only, answering what is asked and nothing more. This is a quiet limit that you do not need to announce.
response_options.disengagement: Decide privately, with an advocate, how and when to change routines, numbers or devices. A sudden change can be noticed, so the order of steps is worth planning.
response_options.support_seeking: Call a domestic violence or stalking helpline and describe what you have noticed. Advocates can help you assess risk, plan, and decide what to document, without you having to decide anything on the call.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Let one trusted person at work, such as security or a manager, know that someone may come to the workplace uninvited, and give them a photo and the key facts. Keep a dated log of any visit or message there.

Stalking & Surveillance (Post-Separation.boundary_script: "For the schedule and the bills, can we keep everything in writing in one place, like email or a co-parenting app? That way neither of us has to guess what was agreed." Offer this through a lawyer, mediator or co-parenting app, and only after an advocate agrees.
Stalking & Surveillance (Post-Separation.safety_note: Danger signals include showing up where you never said you would be, threats, damaged property and knowledge of private conversations. Others are tracking devices and contact that rises after you set a limit or begin a new relationship. Risk can rise around a separation. Before you change numbers, devices or routes, ask a stalking or domestic violence advocate to help you plan the order, since sudden changes can be noticed.
misuse_warning: Reading every run-in, friend's remark or unanswered question as stalking can frighten you more than the facts support. Check how the information could have arrived before deciding.
These words carry legal weight in many places. Using them against a co-parent who is only handling logistics can harm someone who has done nothing wrong.
Stalking & Surveillance (Post-Separation.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Ghosting as Control is absence, a silence that ends when you move on, and stalking is presence or awareness that continues after you ask it to stop. Legal Abuse reaches you through courts and filings with a paper record, where this reaches you through your movements and devices. A Smear Campaign talks about you to others; here the others are mostly being asked about you.

Legal Abuse (Post-Separation).short_definition: Using court filings, motions and hearings after a separation, over and over, in ways that drain the other person's money, time and stability.
Legal Abuse (Post-Separation).core_meaning: Using court filings, motions and hearings after a separation, over and over, in ways that drain the other person's money, time and stability.
Legal Abuse (Post-Separation).expanded_definition: Legal abuse is the repeated use of legitimate court processes, such as custody petitions, motions, contempt filings and requests for hearings, so that responding becomes a heavy burden in itself. Each filing may look ordinary, and a judge may see nothing wrong in any single one. Complicated separations do need several legal steps, so volume alone is weak evidence. The concern arises when settled issues return without new grounds and the cost to one side far outweighs what is being disputed.
Legal Abuse (Post-Separation).plain_language_summary: After a split, someone keeps taking the other person back to court, with filings that look normal one by one, until the cost in money and nerves is the harm.
Legal Abuse (Post-Separation).why_this_matters: Each filing looks procedurally normal on its own, so the cost builds in money, time and nerves without producing one moment anyone would call abuse. Meanwhile the person responding may risk their home, income or time with their children if a deadline is missed.
what_it_is: Court filings, motions, requests for hearings and appeals that return to matters already decided, without new facts or changed circumstances.
Use of timing: papers served close to holidays, exams, a new job or a move, so the response window is short.
Costs that fall unevenly: the person with fewer resources must still answer each document or risk losing by default.
Complaints to agencies or professional bodies that each have to be answered separately.
Found in custody, child support, property and protective-order disputes.
Different from litigation that is merely hard-fought: each side may fight hard and still be using the court for a real question.
what_it_sounds_like: A fourth motion to change the parenting schedule in a year, citing no new events.
Papers delivered the week of your move, with a hearing set two weeks out.
You'll be hearing from my lawyer, again.
A request to re-hear the finances already settled in the agreement.
A filing that accuses you of contempt over a minor, late exchange time.
Another subpoena for records you already provided.
I'm only doing what's best for the kids, said with each new filing.
what_it_is_not: Complicated separations legitimately need many legal steps, such as valuing a business, settling property or setting a parenting plan across several courts.
Courts are slow and expensive by themselves. Delay and cost may come from the system and not from either person.
Someone protecting a real interest, like a child's safety or a financial right, will feel adversarial to the other side.
A genuine request to change an order after circumstances shifted, such as a relocation, a job change or a child's new needs.
Enforcement of an agreement the other person truly has not followed.
this_may_be_it_when: The same issues come back in new papers with nothing that has changed.
Filing dates cluster around events in your life.
You spend more responding than the disputed amount or issue is worth.
Several filings have been declined or dismissed, and new ones follow.
Offers to settle are refused, then the matter returns later in another form.
this_may_not_be_it_when: Each filing cites a new fact, such as a new job, a move or a school change.
Courts have granted at least some of the requests.
Your own lawyer says the volume is routine for cases like yours.
The timeline follows deadlines the court itself set.
The matters in dispute are real, large and unresolved, like a pension or a relocation.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Property, business or support questions can take several rounds because the numbers are truly hard to pin down.
A new lawyer may file procedural papers to bring a file up to date.
Court calendars set dates in bursts, so papers can arrive close together without anyone timing them.
People who feel unheard sometimes file again in the hope that a different judge will listen.
common_false_positives: A long custody case with real disagreements on both sides, run by two lawyers who file regularly.
An appeal of a decision, which is a lawful and routine step.
Notices from the court's own system, such as reminders and scheduling letters, which can feel like attacks.
discernment_questions: Does each filing cite something new, or return to something already decided?
Has a lawyer or legal aid worker looked at the pattern and said whether it is ordinary?
Would the cost of responding make sense if the stakes were as large as the filings say?
Do the dates line up with events in my life more than with any court deadline?
Have any judges commented on the repeated filings?
Can I keep a clean timeline of every filing, date and cost?
less_concerning_if: The court has treated each request as serious and mostly granted it.
The filings are spread out and tied to real changes.
Both sides are filing, and both sides have lawyers.
more_concerning_if: You are missing work, falling behind on rent or borrowing money to respond.
Filings reach into custody time or housing, and a missed deadline could lose either.
A judge has commented on the repeated filings, and they continue.
pattern_over_time_signs: You dread the mailbox, the process server and the email from the court portal.
Each time something settles, new papers arrive within weeks.
Savings or credit are drawn down by legal costs far beyond what you planned.
You agree to terms you dislike to end the filings, not because you think they are fair.
Legal Abuse (Post-Separation).repair_check: Change would show in withdrawn or narrowed filings, a settlement that is honored without return trips to court, and proposals made through lawyers or mediation instead of fresh papers. A friendly message arriving alongside a new motion has changed nothing.
Legal Abuse (Post-Separation).boundary_respect_check: Look at what follows a request to settle a matter through mediation or between lawyers. Agreement and a real drop in filings is one kind of answer. A fresh filing within weeks, or word that the request itself will be raised in court, is the other.
Legal Abuse (Post-Separation).psychological_mechanism: A long process can wear down money, sleep and concentration, and people sometimes begin to accept terms to make the process stop, not because the terms feel fair. Uncertainty about the next filing keeps the body on alert, and every envelope can bring the dread back. The official look of the papers can also make a person feel it must be their fault.
Legal Abuse (Post-Separation).possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe dread over the mail, financial strain, trouble working, and a sense that the case never ends. Some give in on money or parenting time just to stop. Others describe shame about being 'in court again', and anger that every step looked lawful and so nobody saw it as harm.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask your lawyer or a legal aid clinic one question: 'Is this volume of filings ordinary for a case like mine?' An outside professional read helps you tell heavy litigation from a pattern.
response_options.firm_boundary: Respond on time through your lawyer, in writing, keeping replies to the facts. Deadlines are where a stretched person loses the most.
response_options.disengagement: Move all talk about the case to counsel and let lawyers carry the correspondence, so you are not answering personal messages about the filings.
response_options.support_seeking: Seek a legal aid office, a court self-help center or a domestic violence legal advocate. Ask them to read the filings and say what they see.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: Tell one trusted manager only what you need to, such as that you have court dates, and arrange leave in advance, so a hearing does not put your job at risk.

Legal Abuse (Post-Separation).boundary_script: "Anything about the schedule or what has changed, we can talk about directly. For the court matters, could we go through our lawyers, or a mediator, so that everything is in writing and nothing is missed?" Raise this through your lawyer, and only after an advocate or lawyer agrees.
Legal Abuse (Post-Separation).safety_note: Concern grows when filings sit alongside threats, danger to a child, or the chance of losing your home, income or custody time at the next hearing. Courts also hear true accounts of danger, so a filing is not proof of abuse. Bring the full file to a family law attorney or legal aid advocate and ask what limits or protections your court offers.
misuse_warning: Calling a hard-fought custody case legal abuse can dismiss a parent with a real concern about a child's safety. Courts need to hear those.
Reading a hostile lawyer's letter, or a motion you disagree with, as proof of a campaign can harden a case that might have settled.
Legal Abuse (Post-Separation).how_to_distinguish_from_related: Forced Submission presses a person directly for words, while Legal Abuse works through an official channel, where the pressure arrives as paperwork. A Smear Campaign damages reputation among people, whereas filings damage mostly through cost and time, and may become public record. Stalking & Surveillance (Post-Separation) follows a person's movements, but legal filings can arrive without any physical contact.

Edited Recordings.short_definition: Presenting a cut, trimmed or out-of-context recording as if it were the whole, so that it seems to prove more than the full version supports.
Edited Recordings.core_meaning: Presenting a cut, trimmed or out-of-context recording as if it were the whole, so that it seems to prove more than the full version supports.
Edited Recordings.expanded_definition: Edited recordings are real audio or video, cut, rearranged or clipped so that they seem to show something the full version does not. The recording is usually genuine, unlike a deepfake that fabricates speech or faces, but the cut changes what it seems to prove. Trimming for length is normal, and a short clip labeled as a clip is honest. The concern is an excerpt offered as the whole, or a splice that joins words that were never said together.
Edited Recordings.plain_language_summary: A real recording that has been trimmed or stitched so it seems to show something the whole thing does not.
Edited Recordings.why_this_matters: A recording carries the authority of evidence, so the burden falls on the person in it to talk their way out of something that appears to show itself. An explanation of the missing context rarely travels as far as the clip did.
what_it_is: A genuine recording that has been cropped, trimmed, spliced or re-ordered, so the meaning shifts.
A clip that starts after the provocation or ends before the reply, so the response seems to come from nowhere.
Words from different moments joined into one sentence, or pauses removed so a hesitation looks like an admission.
Shared in disputes, workplace complaints, custody conflicts, group chats, social media posts and news clips.
Different from a deepfake: nothing is invented, so checking the original is the best test.
what_it_sounds_like: A call recording that begins mid-argument, with no sign of who raised their voice first.
A video that jumps at the exact second before an explanation.
A transcript whose line numbers skip, or timestamps with gaps.
A voice memo played aloud with 'listen, he admits it', stopping one second before the next sentence.
A clip said to be 'the full conversation' that runs two minutes when the call lasted forty.
Background sound that changes in tone or volume mid-sentence.
You remember the moment, and the clip does not sound like what happened.
what_it_is_not: Clips shortened for length and clarity. An excerpt honestly labeled as partial makes no claim to be the whole picture.
Poor recording quality and natural gaps in a device's capture, such as a phone that stopped when its storage ran out.
A highlight reel or summary that says it is a summary.
Two honest recordings of the same event from different angles that show different parts of it.
A genuine, complete recording of something you wish you had not said. Being quoted accurately is uncomfortable, but it is not editing.
this_may_be_it_when: The clip begins or ends exactly where context would change the meaning.
There is an unexplained jump in sound, lighting or background at a key moment.
The person presenting it will not share the original file, or says they do not have it.
It is described as complete but is much shorter than the event it comes from.
Other people who were present remember a different order or tone than the clip shows.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The clip is labeled as an excerpt, with a source and a link to the full version.
The full recording is available and says the same thing.
The jumps are explained by how the app or device works, such as pausing for silence.
Others who were there recall it the way the clip shows it.
The only thing you can find wrong is that you dislike what it shows.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Phones and meeting apps trim silence or stop recording on their own, which can leave gaps.
People cut clips to fit a platform's time limit without thinking about context.
Someone with a long recording may share only the part they found relevant, assuming the rest was not needed.
Compression and noise reduction can make audio sound spliced when it is not.
common_false_positives: A news report using a ten-second quote that is faithful to the longer speech.
A meeting recording that cut off when the call dropped.
A recording of a heated moment that sounds worse on its own than it felt in the room, but contains everything that was said.
discernment_questions: Is there a complete version, and who holds it?
Where does the clip begin and end, and what was said just before and just after?
Is the clip labeled as an excerpt, or presented as the full record?
Do the jumps in sound or picture land on the most important sentence?
Would the people who were there describe it the way the clip does?
Could someone neutral check the file's original?
less_concerning_if: The excerpt is clearly marked, and the full version is easy to get.
The person sharing it provides the full recording once asked.
People who were there confirm the clip's gist.
more_concerning_if: The clip is being used against you in a complaint, a legal matter or a public post, and the original is withheld.
It is circulating widely before anyone can check it.
Your recollection, and that of several others, differs sharply from what the clip implies.
pattern_over_time_signs: Short clips of you keep appearing and the full versions never do.
You have started recording your own conversations out of worry about what might be cut.
People quote a line back to you that you say you never said that way.
Each time you ask for the original, it is described as lost, deleted or unavailable.
Edited Recordings.repair_check: Fixing it means the full recording is produced, the clip is corrected or taken down wherever it was posted, and the people who saw it are told. A comment saying 'sorry if that was unclear' while the clip stays up leaves the effect in place.
Edited Recordings.boundary_respect_check: Ask for the full file, or the timestamps on either side of the clip. Watch whether it arrives with an explanation, or whether the question is met with 'why do you need it?' and the clip travels further.
Edited Recordings.psychological_mechanism: Audio and video are often treated as direct evidence, so a clip can persuade before anyone asks what was left out. A first impression of a clip can also stick after a longer version is seen. Missing context leaves viewers to fill the gap with their own assumptions, often the least generous ones.
Edited Recordings.possible_impact_on_receiver: Seeing themselves quoted brings a drop in the stomach, then a scramble to explain, and tiredness from explaining to each new audience. Some start to doubt their own memory of the event. Others pull out of group chats, workplaces or platforms where the clip has circulated.

response_options.soft_clarification: Ask the person sharing it for the full recording and the times where the clip begins and ends: 'Can I hear the whole thing, starting from a few minutes earlier?'
response_options.firm_boundary: Decline to argue about the clip's meaning until the full recording is on the table: 'I'm happy to discuss what was said once we've both heard all of it.'
response_options.disengagement: Do not reshare or reply to the clip in public threads, which gives it more reach. Save a copy and a link for later use.
response_options.support_seeking: Play the clip and the full version for a friend who was not there, without telling them what you think, and ask what each leaves them believing.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: In a complaint process, ask the investigator in writing to obtain the original, complete, unedited file and its metadata, and attach your own written account of the missing part.

Edited Recordings.boundary_script: "Could we hear the whole recording, from before this starts to after it ends? Once we've both listened to all of it, we can talk about what was said."
Edited Recordings.safety_note: A doctored clip is not a danger by itself. What changes that is its use as leverage: a threat to send it to your employer, family or a court unless you comply, or a clip tied to intimate content. In that case, keep the evidence, hold off on replying, and take it to a lawyer or advocate who can advise on the next step.
misuse_warning: Calling any unflattering clip edited lets you dismiss what you actually said. Check whether something you can point to is missing before accusing anyone.
Insisting that someone produce a recording they never made, or that no longer exists, treats a missing file as proof of bad faith.
Edited Recordings.how_to_distinguish_from_related: A Smear Campaign spreads claims, true or false, about a person and may use no recording at all, while an edited recording gives a claim a piece of apparent proof. Legal Abuse can bring such a clip into a court filing, whereas an edited recording is about how the clip was cut. Forced Submission demands words from you, but an edited clip can put words in your mouth without your input.

SIM Swap / 2FA Interception.short_definition: Taking over a person's phone number, or the text codes sent to it, to get into their accounts, lock them out or read their messages.
SIM Swap / 2FA Interception.core_meaning: Taking over a person's phone number, or the text codes sent to it, to get into their accounts, lock them out or read their messages.
SIM Swap / 2FA Interception.expanded_definition: A SIM swap is when a phone number is moved onto a different SIM card than the owner's, so calls and texts go to someone else. 2FA interception is the wider outcome: the one-time codes that prove who you are reach another person, by a swap or by other routes. Carrier outages and glitches happen, so one odd code means little. The telltale run is a lost signal, followed by lockouts and by account changes that someone else made.
SIM Swap / 2FA Interception.plain_language_summary: Someone gets control of your phone number or the codes sent to it, then uses them to get into your accounts while you are locked out.
SIM Swap / 2FA Interception.why_this_matters: The phone number that secures everything else becomes the way in, and the lockout usually arrives before there is any way to understand what has happened. Email, banking and messaging can all be reached from a single number, so a loss can spread quickly.
what_it_is: A phone number moved to a SIM or device the owner does not hold, which takes over their calls and texts.
Text-message codes that arrive with someone else, so they can pass the checks for logins and password resets.
Often arranged through a carrier's account processes and not by breaking into your device.
Used for theft, impersonation, reading private messages, or cutting a person off from their own accounts, and sometimes by someone the person knows.
Two overlapping behaviors: swapping is one method, interception of codes is the broader result, and interception can also happen without a swap.
what_it_sounds_like: Your phone suddenly shows 'No service' or 'SOS only' in a place where you normally have full bars.
Texts with verification codes you did not ask for, arriving in a bunch.
An email from your carrier saying your SIM or number was changed, which you did not do.
A bank alert about a password reset, a new payee or a login from a device you do not own.
Friends telling you they received odd messages from your number or account.
Being signed out of email and social accounts at once, with the recovery address changed.
A call or text from 'your carrier' asking you to read out a code.
what_it_is_not: Carriers have outages, tower maintenance and billing errors that drop service for hours.
A single odd authentication code on one platform, which often means someone mistyped their own address.
A SIM replacement you asked for yourself, after a lost or broken phone or an upgrade, that you forgot in a stressful week.
A line moved to a new plan or eSIM by a family-plan owner who legitimately manages the account.
Travel or roaming problems that cut service when you cross a border.
this_may_be_it_when: Service drops without explanation and the carrier later confirms a SIM or number change you did not request.
Several unrelated accounts show resets or sign-ins from new devices within the same day.
The recovery phone number or email on an account has been changed without you.
Texts or calls meant for you stop arriving at your phone.
The timing matches a falling-out with someone who had access to your carrier account or devices, which shows only access and not who acted.
this_may_not_be_it_when: The carrier confirms an outage or maintenance in your area, and service returns on its own.
Your carrier's account history shows only changes you or the account owner made.
Only one platform is affected, and everything else works.
Codes arrive when you are actually trying to sign in.
The lockout comes from too many password attempts and clears after a wait or a verification.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: Phone carriers drop service for outages and repairs, often without notice.
People forget their own SIM or eSIM changes when moving to a new phone.
Family-plan owners can legitimately change numbers and lines on the account.
Apps send codes automatically whenever anyone, including a stranger mistyping an address, enters yours.
common_false_positives: Service cut after a missed bill payment.
Verification codes sent because a bot or stranger entered your number in a sign-up form.
A new phone that took a few hours to register your number properly.
discernment_questions: Has my carrier confirmed an account change that someone other than me requested?
Did my signal vanish around the same time that accounts began to lock?
Are the changes to recovery emails and numbers ones I made?
Who else has ever had access to my carrier account, number or devices?
Is it one account or many, and did it begin all at once?
Do bank alerts or messages from friends show activity I did not do?
less_concerning_if: The carrier shows an outage, a billing hold or a change you made.
Only one service is affected and the others work normally.
Service returns within hours and your accounts show nothing unfamiliar.
more_concerning_if: Money has moved, or new payees, cards or limits have appeared at your bank or card account.
Your recovery email or number on accounts has changed, or messages are being forwarded.
Someone from your past with access to your plan or devices has already shown knowledge of your private messages.
pattern_over_time_signs: Accounts keep being re-accessed after you reset passwords.
Your messages seem known to someone outside the conversation.
Verification codes arrive repeatedly for logins you did not attempt.
Friends report unusual messages that look as if they came from you, more than once.
SIM Swap / 2FA Interception.repair_check: Resolution looks like the carrier confirming it has reversed the change and added extra protection to the line, each account recovering with a clean sign-in history, and no new unexplained codes over the following weeks. Regaining one login while the number stays exposed is only a partial fix.
SIM Swap / 2FA Interception.boundary_respect_check: Treat the weeks after you tighten security as the test. If codes stop arriving and sign-in histories stay clean, the change held. If lockouts return, new-device alerts reappear, or someone seems to know about changes you only made privately, treat access as still open and contact your carrier's fraud team.
SIM Swap / 2FA Interception.psychological_mechanism: Losing the number that proves who you are can resemble losing your identity at once, since email, money and friends all hang from it. Rapid, unexplained lockouts tend to push people to act fast, and urgency makes it harder to sort real alerts from fake ones. Messages posing as 'your bank' or 'your carrier' can take advantage of that urgency.
SIM Swap / 2FA Interception.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe panic when the signal vanishes, then dread as accounts lock one by one. Some lose money or access to years of photos and messages. Others feel exposed in the days afterward, afraid of what was read, and distrust their own phone. When someone known to them is involved, they describe an added sense of betrayal.

response_options.soft_clarification: Check first from a different, trusted device or a friend's phone: look at your carrier account's recent changes and at the sign-in history on your email. Write down what you find, with times.
response_options.firm_boundary: Do not read out codes or PINs to anyone who calls or texts, even if they seem to be your carrier or bank. Hang up and contact them through the number on your card or their official app.
response_options.disengagement: Once you are back in control, move key accounts such as email and banking off text-message codes, where the service allows, onto an authenticator app or a physical security key.
response_options.support_seeking: Contact your carrier's fraud team, your bank and, where one exists, your country's fraud reporting service. If an ex-partner may be involved, also speak to a domestic abuse or stalking advocate.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If a work account is affected, tell the IT or security team right away, and treat any message sent from your number or email during that window as suspect.

SIM Swap / 2FA Interception.boundary_script: "I did not request a change to my SIM or my number. Please note that on the account, require extra verification for any future change, and send me a written record of what changed and when."
SIM Swap / 2FA Interception.safety_note: Danger signals include money moving, access to your private messages, or messages that show someone knows your movements, especially a former partner who once held your carrier details. A SIM problem in that setting may be one piece of wider monitoring. Contact your carrier and bank from a device that person has never touched, and reach a stalking or domestic abuse advocate before changing anything they might notice.
misuse_warning: Reading a one-off dropped signal or a stray verification code as a SIM swap can cause alarm that the facts do not support. The first check is your carrier's account history.
Pointing at a particular person from nothing but timing can turn a technical fraud into a family or workplace accusation.
SIM Swap / 2FA Interception.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Stalking & Surveillance (Post-Separation) is the watching of a former partner's life, and a SIM swap can be a route to it by sending that person's messages and codes elsewhere, but strangers also do it for money with no personal link. Legal Abuse works through courts and paper, in the open, while a swap works quietly through accounts and is found by what stops working. Forced Submission needs the person's own words, where a swap takes control with no input from them.

Intimate Image Abuse.short_definition: Sharing or threatening to share private sexual images of someone without consent, including fake ones, often tied to a demand for money, contact or compliance.
Intimate Image Abuse.core_meaning: Sharing or threatening to share private sexual images of someone without consent, including fake ones, often tied to a demand for money, contact or compliance.
Intimate Image Abuse.expanded_definition: Intimate image abuse covers real or fabricated sexual images used against the person shown: posted, sent on, or threatened with exposure. The threat can be attached to a demand for money, more images, contact or silence, or can follow a breakup. Images shared willingly within trust do not become abuse by existing; the line is passed when they are spread or held over the person without consent. Fear of exposure can steer behavior whether or not anything is shared, and a bluff has the same effect.
Intimate Image Abuse.plain_language_summary: Someone shares, or says they will share, private sexual pictures or videos of you without your agreement, sometimes real and sometimes faked.
Intimate Image Abuse.why_this_matters: Control over the most private material about a person passes to somebody else, and the fear of exposure keeps working whether or not anything is ever actually shared. The shame it brings often leads people to hide it, which is when help is hardest to reach.
what_it_is: Real images shared, posted or sent onward without the consent of the person shown.
Threats to share, with or without a stated demand, that keep the person afraid even if nothing is ever sent.
Fabricated or altered images, such as a face placed on another body, used in the same way.
A claim to hold images that may not exist; the fear and pressure still land, though the response steps differ.
Seen after breakups, in sextortion scams run by strangers, and sometimes inside ongoing relationships.
Often tied to a demand: money, more images, contact, silence or compliance with something else.
what_it_sounds_like: Send me what I ask, or everyone in your contacts sees these.
I still have the pictures, you know.
A message with a screenshot of the picture, your contacts list and a countdown.
Nice to see you've moved on. Maybe your new boyfriend should see what I have.
A fake explicit image of you, with your name on it, posted in a group chat.
Pay now and I'll delete everything. I swear.
An unknown account posting your pictures beside a link to your workplace page.
what_it_is_not: Images shared consensually inside a relationship, with no threat and no sharing beyond it.
Adults who agreed to publish or sell their own content, such as a creator or a couple who chose to post together.
An accidental send to the wrong chat that the recipient deletes at once and tells you about.
Someone telling you that they came across an image of you posted by a third party, so that you can report it, with no demand attached.
A vague line like 'I have stuff on you' with no mention of images, which is a different kind of threat.
this_may_be_it_when: A specific threat names the images, who would see them and what you must do to stop it.
Images appear, or are shown to others, that you did not agree to share.
The threat starts, or returns, after you end contact or begin a new relationship.
An unknown account contacts you after a private chat and shows part of your image or your contact list.
A fake explicit image of you circulates, whether or not you ever took a photo.
this_may_not_be_it_when: Nothing has been shared or threatened, and the images were given in a relationship that remains on good terms.
The message is a vague boast with no mention of images, who would see them or what you must do.
The only images are ones a couple openly agreed to keep, with a shared understanding of what they are for.
Everyone shown agreed to the use, with no pressure.
The message went to hundreds of people as a template and no real image of you was ever included, though it is still worth reporting.
innocent_or_ordinary_possibilities: A partner may keep photos you willingly shared, with no plan to do anything with them.
Pictures sent to the wrong chat by accident can spread because someone forgot to delete them.
A hacked cloud account can expose images even though nobody you know chose to share them.
Two people in a loving relationship may exchange images that stay private for years.
common_false_positives: A friend joking 'I have embarrassing pictures of you' about a clothed vacation photo.
A scam message sent to thousands of strangers saying 'I recorded you', with no real image of you. It is still a threat to report, but it is not a leak.
A relative posting a swimsuit photo from a family vacation, which may be tactless but is not sexual exposure.
discernment_questions: Has anything actually been posted or sent, or is it a threat so far?
Is a demand attached, such as money, more images or contact, and does it keep changing?
Do I know the images exist, or only that someone says they do?
Who could have copies, and could one of my accounts have been breached?
Is the threat tied to something I am doing, such as ending contact?
Do I have a safe place to save screenshots and links?
less_concerning_if: No image exists or has been shown, and the message is generic and sent to many people.
The images stayed private after an amicable end.
A copy was removed from the platform where it appeared, and you can see the link no longer works.
more_concerning_if: Images have been shared or shown to people who matter to you, such as family, an employer or a school.
The demands escalate, a deadline is set, or contact arrives from several accounts.
You feel unsafe in person, or the threat comes with other controlling behavior, such as monitoring, stalking or control of money.
pattern_over_time_signs: The reference returns whenever you pull away: 'remember what I have.'
You change what you post, who you see or your job search out of fear of what could appear.
Demands shift from one thing to another, and each payment or image buys only a pause.
You have started to check search results, group chats and tagged posts for your own pictures.
Intimate Image Abuse.repair_check: Repair shows in things you can see for yourself: posts taken down, links that now fail, and threats that stop and do not come back. A promise to delete with nothing visible behind it leaves the option open, and so does an apology that arrives alongside a new demand.
Intimate Image Abuse.boundary_respect_check: A limit on this subject is judged by the next message. A reply that ends the threat, followed by a gap that holds, is one kind. A larger demand, a deadline, or a copy sent to someone close to you is the other, and that is the point to stop replying and reach a helpline or advocate.
Intimate Image Abuse.psychological_mechanism: Fear of exposure works through shame and the picture of everyone you know seeing it. The threat does not need to be carried out to work, because imagining it can be enough. Secrecy tends to deepen the hold: the longer a person handles it alone, the more the other party's control can feel total, and each demand can feel smaller than the feared exposure.
Intimate Image Abuse.possible_impact_on_receiver: People describe panic, nausea, shame, trouble sleeping and a feeling of being watched wherever they go. Some stop using social media or avoid work and school for fear of being recognized. Many describe relief once they told one person, and some describe anger at being blamed for taking the picture in the first place.

response_options.soft_clarification: Before replying, save everything: screenshots of messages, usernames, links and dates, stored somewhere private. Questions and arguments with the sender can wait until you have advice.
response_options.firm_boundary: Do not pay, send more images or negotiate. Payment or new images tend to bring further demands, not an end. Further contact with the sender can wait until an advocate has advised; do not send them the wording below.
response_options.disengagement: If the sender is someone you know, ask an advocate before blocking or going silent, since a sudden change can raise the pressure. With a stranger, blocking after saving evidence is usually fine.
response_options.support_seeking: Tell someone you trust and contact an image-abuse helpline or advocate. StopNCII.org (adults) and Take It Down (images taken before 18, even if you are now an adult) let you flag an image so participating platforms can block it, without sharing it.
response_options.workplace_or_professional: If images or threats reach your job or school, tell one trusted person in HR, student services or security early, so it does not arrive as a surprise. Give them the links, not the images.

Intimate Image Abuse.boundary_script: "I did not agree to these images being shared. I have saved the links, messages and dates, and I am asking for help getting them removed." Send this to a platform, school, employer or advocate, never to the person who shared them.
Intimate Image Abuse.safety_note: Take seriously a deadline, a demand that keeps growing, contact from several accounts, messages to your family or workplace, or threats of self-harm used to keep you quiet. If shame feels unbearable, a crisis line can help tonight. If the person shown is under 18, treat it as urgent and contact your country's child-safety or police service. Save links and screenshots, then ask an advocate about takedown options before replying.
misuse_warning: Using the label for any private picture someone still has can accuse a former partner of abuse when nothing has been threatened or shared. The line is consent and use, not possession.
Treating the person shown as responsible because they once took or sent the picture adds blame to someone who needs help. The picture existing is not the wrongdoing.
Intimate Image Abuse.how_to_distinguish_from_related: Public Humiliation exposes someone in front of others, though not necessarily with sexual material or an attached demand. Forced Submission presses a person to say words, while intimate image abuse presses with a threat of exposure and may ask for money or more images instead. Stalking & Surveillance (Post-Separation) may sit alongside it, but concerns following and watching, not the exposure of private images.
